[PATH:empirical] A field experiment comparing self-reported weekly productivity logs with actual keystroke and task-completion data from a remote-work software firm (e.g., using a platform like Time Doctor or Hubstaff). — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing subjective reports against objective tracking, controlling for task type and job role.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies (2020–2023) on self-report bias in remote work productivity, focusing on effect sizes and moderators like manager feedback frequency. — Synthesizes available evidence to determine whether overestimation is systematic, and identifies gaps in current research.

[PATH:empirical] Survey-based study with embedded validation questions (e.g., asking participants to recall specific tasks and cross-referencing with digital trace data from collaboration tools like Slack and Jira). — Provides a scalable method to detect overestimation patterns across multiple organizations, while controlling for memory decay and social desirability bias.

[PATH:empirical] Meta-analysis of field experiments comparing self-reported productivity to objectively measured output (e.g., keystroke logs, task completion rates) in remote vs. office settings — Directly tests the discrepancy between self-reports and objective metrics, providing causal evidence on overestimation bias in remote work.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey study with matched employee-manager dyads tracking self-assessed productivity and manager-rated performance over 12+ months post-pandemic — Captures temporal dynamics and cross-rater divergence, assessing whether overestimation persists or corrects with experience.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework from behavioral economics on self-serving bias and social desirability in performance self-reports, applied to remote work contexts — Provides mechanistic grounding for why overestimation occurs, guiding hypothesis refinement and testable predictions.

C006.subject: automated digital activity tracking metrics in remote work environments
C006.object: actual output for knowledge workers performing complex, non-linear tasks
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: automated digital activity tracking metrics in remote work environments actual output for knowledge workers performing complex, non-linear tasks]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled lab study comparing self-reported output logs with continuous keystroke/mouse activity data for knowledge workers completing complex analytical tasks over a workweek — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring the discrepancy between actual output (e.g., reports, insights) and metrics based solely on continuous input events, controlling for planning and offline thinking periods.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study in a remote software development team using IDE plugins and time-tracking software, paired with daily diary entries capturing planning, reading, and offline cognitive work — Provides ecologically valid evidence of how input-based metrics underestimate actual output when non-linear tasks involve significant offline cognitive phases, addressing the condition specified in the qualifier.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of cognitive science literature on the role of incubation and offline processing in complex problem-solving (e.g., Wagner et al., 2004; Schooler et al., 1993) — Establishes theoretical grounding that planning and offline thinking are critical for complex task output, supporting the plausibility that input-only metrics would systematically underestimate actual productivity.

qualifier.condition: when metrics rely solely on continuous input events and exclude planning, reading, or offline thinking periods

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of productivity studies comparing self-reported output vs. keystroke/activity metrics in remote vs. office settings (e.g., Bloom et al., 2021; Choudhury et al., 2021) — Provides aggregated empirical evidence on whether automated tracking metrics correlate with actual output across different work environments, controlling for task type and measurement bias.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment in a multinational corporation randomly assigning employees to remote and office conditions, with both automated activity logs and manager-rated output KPIs — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing the correspondence between tracking metrics and actual output under controlled conditions, isolating the effect of measurement modality.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework on algorithmic management and measurement reactivity (e.g., Kellogg et al., 2020; Bernstein, 2017) applied to remote work — Explains why tracking metrics may systematically misrepresent output due to gaming, context insensitivity, or differential effort allocation, informing the plausibility of the hypothesis.
